DESCRIPTION: The convergence layer declares success on pure emptiness. `validate_no_findings()` says the convention should be “not converged unless null_expected”, but the actual implementation gives empty rounds `kappa_set=1`, `kappa_rate=1`, `kappa_adopt=1`, so `converged(2)` becomes `True`. I verified this with a read-only probe: three empty rounds returned `1.0 1.0 1.0 True`. In the full manager path, that lets `process_round()` terminate the FSM as `CONVERGED` with zero evidence.

REF: [dynamic_management.py:2115](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2115), [dynamic_management.py:2572](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2572), [dynamic_management.py:2788](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2788)  
DESCRIPTION: Most recovery actions are computed and then dropped on the floor. `FailureHandler.get_recovery()` can choose `RETRY_EXTENDED`, `RETRY_CLARIFIED`, `DEGRADE`, or `DOWNGRADE_ROLE`, but `DynamicManager.process_round()` only uses the returned `action` to set `critical_failure` for `ABORT`. `RoundResult` does not expose the chosen recovery action, and no recovery events are emitted here either. Operationally, the public orchestrator interface hides or ignores most of the recovery policy table.

REF: [dynamic_management.py:2744](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2744), [dynamic_management.py:2804](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2804), [dynamic_management.py:2865](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2865)  
DESCRIPTION: `process_round()` performs no integrity checks on incoming payloads. It does not verify that response/finding `model_id`s belong to the managed pool, and it does not verify that `response.round_idx` / `finding.round_idx` match the FSM’s current round. I verified this with a probe: a foreign model id `ghost` and round `99` were accepted unchanged, stored in `RoundResult.responses`, and the foreign finding entered convergence classes. That means stale or injected payloads can corrupt failure history, convergence, diminishing-returns, and adaptive fingerprint state.

REF: [dynamic_management.py:1421](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:1421), [dynamic_management.py:2579](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2579), [dynamic_management.py:2865](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2865), [dynamic_management.py:2936](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:2936)  
DESCRIPTION: Historical round state is not snapshotted; it is retained through caller-owned mutable objects. `RoundResult` stores the original `findings` list and `responses` dict by reference, and `ConvergenceDetector.add_round_findings()` only makes a shallow list copy of `Finding` objects. I verified one concrete consequence: after `process_round()`, appending to the caller’s original `findings` list changed `len(mgr.round_results[0].findings)` from 1 to 2. Because later rounds read `_round_results` to build prior-finding state, outside mutation can silently rewrite the manager’s past.

REF: [dynamic_management.py:781](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:781), [dynamic_management.py:837](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:837), [dynamic_management.py:910](/Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering/bench/dynamic_management.py:910)  
DESCRIPTION: The load-balancing diagnostics mask zero-capacity overloads as benign. `_objective()` and `_balanced()` treat any model with `L <= 0` as having load fraction `0.0`, even if it was force-assigned work. I verified this with a probe: one model with `L=0` and one task produced an infeasible allocation `[[1]]`, raised an F1 warning, yet still returned finite cost `10.0` and `balanced=True`, while `Allocation.model_load_fraction()` for the same model was `inf`. So the summary metrics can make an impossible allocation look healthy.

DESCRIPTION: PM aborts do not deactivate the PM in the reported active set. For repeated PM transport/protocol failures, `get_recovery()` returns `ABORT` but does not remove the PM from `_active_models`; only `EXCLUDE` does that. I verified directly that after `RecoveryAction.ABORT`, `active_models` still contains the failed PM. The run still terminates, but `active_models` and `RoundResult.active_models` misreport which models were actually still viable at the abort point.
